{"content": " 251|

They dated, drifted apart, and later reconnected briefly, as young people often do when life opens into wider distances. Eventually Bob heard that Barb had married and gone to Iran. Then the Iranian Revolution came in 1979, the Shah fell, communication with America constricted, and whatever thread had remained between them effectively snapped. Bob never knew for certain what became of her. He only knew that history, which feels abstract in textbooks, can close over an ordinary life like water over a dropped stone. His first crush became part of his education in loss—small compared to what would come later, but real.

252|

The Moonshot

253|

Space had already entered Bob's imagination in layers. Sputnik had announced that the sky was no longer untouchable. Yuri Gagarin and Alan Shepard made spaceflight something human beings could actually do. Then in July of 1969 Bob sat with his family in front of the television and watched Neil Armstrong step onto the moon. The image was grainy. The signal ghosted and shimmered. None of that mattered. A man had crossed a quarter of a million miles of emptiness, descended in a fragile machine, and climbed down a ladder into history.

254|

For Bob the moon landing was not merely a patriotic triumph or a technological spectacle. It was proof that ambitious cooperation could drag the impossible into the realm of the accomplished. It confirmed something he had already begun to suspect: the future belonged to builders, to engineers, to people willing to do hard things on behalf of visions larger than themselves. He did not yet know exactly where his own career would lead, but from that night forward it leaned unmistakably toward the sky.

255|

The Weight of Expectation

256|

College acceptance brought new pressures. Bob was going to be the first in his family to attend university—a milestone that carried both opportunity and obligation. His father and mother and for that matter the rest of the neighborhood could not visualize anyone going to college at first. One of the adult neighbors told Bob he was wasting his time—no one from that neighborhood had the money or class to be a college student. His mother was quieter about it, but Bob could see the worry in her eyes. She understood something his father didn't: that education changed people, that the boy who went away might not be the same man who returned. She was proud, deeply proud, but also afraid of losing him to a world she didn't understand. "Don't forget who you are," she told him the night before he left for campus. "Don't forget where you came from. The world you're entering—it has different values than ours. Money matters more there. Status matters more. Don't let them convince you that we're simple or stupid because we didn't go to college. Your father and I did the best we could with what we had."

257|

Bob promised, not fully understanding what he was promising. He was eighteen, eager to escape the constraints of his upbringing, hungry for the knowledge and experiences that awaited him. The caution his mother offered felt like a weight he didn't want to carry.

258|

Walk About

259|

There's something about walking—really walking, for hours on end—that changes the way you think about the world. It's not exercise. It's not transportation. It's a different way of being in the world, a slower pace that lets your mind catch up with your body.

260|

When I was nineteen, I took a walk about. Not the Australian kind, where you walk through the Outback and come face to face with your own mortality. I mean the American kind, where you just... go. Bob gathered a couple of guy friends, and they just started walking—starting in a Lake Michigan beach town and with backpacks in hand they started following the coast north. For six days they walked until they reached a place where the sand dunes disappeared into the water and they could go no further. They walked through beaches, over sand dunes and through farmland. It was cathartic.

261|

Michigan State University

262|

At the time the Vietnam war raged on and in his senior year of high school Bob received a low draft number in the national draft lottery. This meant he was bound for combat in the rice paddies of Vietnam. A few days later he received a letter from a government agency—they needed electronics technicians and offered Bob an alternative, a small scholarship and relief from the draft in exchange for occasional work overseas. Bob discussed this with his father who had a very practical view. He said, "If you're given an opportunity to serve your country in a way less likely to get you killed, take it." So Bob did—that is another story for another time.

263|

After high school Bob went to community college because he could live at home and work, earning enough for tuition. Bob enrolled at Michigan State University in the following fall, choosing it over the University of Michigan because of a spring high school college visit. Bob and a friend first went to the University of Michigan, they rushed between buildings and were totally convinced that it was the best choice. The next weekend his friend said "let's check out Michigan State." Bob was convinced that the University of Michigan was the best choice but went because of his friend. They spent the morning with a tour that convinced Bob that Michigan State was a good second choice but… Then by lunch the tour was over and Bob and his friend sat by the river in a beautiful gardenscape and 2 co-eds sat down by them and so Bob picked Michigan State. It is strange how small effects can change the direction of your life.

264|

When he started Michigan State there were students from backgrounds he couldn't comprehend. There were kids from wealthy families who talked about summers in Europe, who drove sports cars their parents had bought them, who treated education as an entitlement rather than a privilege. Bob's parents didn't have the money to help much. Bob arrived with a single suitcase, a slide rule his father had given him and his bicycle, and just enough in savings from his TV shop wages to cover the first semester. He worked in the physics lab to cover his room and board and at night repairing TVs. The scholarship covered a little of tuition, but nothing else. He learned to live lean, to make do, to stretch resources the way his mother had taught him.

265|

The coursework was demanding in ways that high school hadn't prepared him for. Physics and calculus consumed hours each day, problem sets that needed not just calculation but genuine understanding of underlying principles. Bob discovered that he had gaps in his preparation—his community college hadn't covered some topics and he spent extra hours teaching himself what others already knew. But he also discovered that his practical experience gave him advantages the other students lacked. When they struggled to visualize electron flow in a circuit, Bob had spent years tracing it through actual televisions. When they puzzled over feedback systems in control theory, he had built servomechanisms in the garage with his father. The abstract mathematics came alive for him in ways that surprised his professors. Dr. Ellenberg, who taught circuit theory, called Bob to his office after a particularly creative solution to a filter design problem. "Where did you learn to think like this? This isn't from the textbook." That conversation stuck with Bob. It confirmed the years in the garage, the summers at the TV shop, the random accumulation of practical skills. He was not behind—he was different, approaching the same destination from another path. The challenge was integrating the two: formal education and hands-on experience, theory and intuition, the analytical precision of engineering and the creative problem-solving he had learned at his father's workbench.

266|

Paying for School

267|

Bob funded college the hard way. Money determined how many credits he could risk each term, which meant education was never an abstraction. It was measured in hours worked, shifts covered, and whether the previous semester's wages could carry the next one. He started in community college because that was what reality allowed. TV repair helped. So did a short-lived job as a junior computer operator at the headquarters of a department-store chain, though that ended quickly when Bob paid more attention to how the computers worked than to the punched-card routines he had been hired to manage. It was a very Bob way to get fired.

268|

After that he worked in a machine shop and learned to use manual mills and other tools in the pre-CNC era, when precision depended on the hands and judgment of the operator rather than software. By day he made metal parts. By night he repaired televisions. The arrangement was exhausting and clarifying. It taught Bob that intelligence mattered, but endurance did too.

269|

Dr. Chen's Laboratory

270|

At Michigan State, opportunity arrived in the form of Dr. Chen, who needed an engineer more than he needed another theoretician. Bob entered a high-energy physics laboratory as the only non-physics student in a room full of graduate students struggling to build a particle calorimeter for experiments connected to Fermilab. The apparatus was huge and unforgiving: heavy iron plates, sensor arrays, noble gas, photonic detection, interfaces that all had to work together if subatomic chaos was ever going to become meaningful data.

271|

Bob's advantage was not deeper knowledge of particle theory. It was practical leadership. He could break a giant technical problem into manageable parts, keep people moving, and refuse to be intimidated by complexity. Over two years the machine took shape, was moved from Michigan State to Chicago, and helped sort the products of collisions at Fermilab. For a junior engineer it was an extraordinary apprenticeship. It also led directly to the next chapter of his life.

272|

Mindy

273|

College also brought Mindy, Bob's first serious girlfriend. He met her through a trio of roommates with whom he began having lunch, and of the three it was Mindy who drew him in. They dated, danced off campus, and inhabited that particular college tenderness in which two people begin to imagine futures alongside one another without yet understanding how differently those futures may unfold.

274|

Mindy wanted to be a doctor, and Bob admired both the ambition and the discipline behind it. When medical-school applications and scholarship interviews arrived, he helped her prepare essays, rehearse answers, and sharpen the way she presented herself. She got in. He was proud of her. But success has its own centrifugal force. Medicine demanded more of her. His early career demanded more of him. Gradually the relationship loosened under the pressure of two serious young lives pulling toward different callings. A year later he brought Christmas gifts, shared a final conversation and a goodbye kiss, and understood that some endings arrive quietly, without betrayal, simply because time has chosen separate roads.

275|

The Camping Trip

276|

There was also a college camping trip to Canada that sounded more straightforward in the planning than it proved to be in reality. Bob and his roommate had expected a simple men's adventure. Then two coeds overheard them talking in the campus café and asked to join. By the time tents were pitched and the social geometry clarified itself, it was obvious that assumptions had been made all around. The girl Bob had hoped to spend time with had chosen his roommate instead.

277|

The rest of the trip was cold, awkward, and memorable for all the wrong reasons—unexpected weather, uncomfortable silences, and the dawning realization that poor communication can freeze a group faster than snowfall. The wilderness was not the only thing that felt exposed. Bob learned something useful anyway: when relationships enter a situation, guessing is a terrible substitute for talking.

278|

The Computer Revolution Accelerates

279|

By Bob's sophomore year, the world was changing faster than the curriculum could keep up. Integrated circuits were replacing vacuum tubes, shrinking computers from room-sized mainframes to machines that sat on desks. The university acquired a PDP-8, a minicomputer that students could actually touch, program, learn from. Bob spent time he could not spare in the computer center. He learned assembly language, then higher-level languages as they emerged. He wrote programs that solved engineering problems, that simulated physical systems, that demonstrated principles he was learning in his other classes. The computer became a tool for understanding, a way to explore ideas that would have been impossibly time-consuming to work through by hand. He also saw the commercial potential. Companies were desperate for people who understood both hardware and software, who could bridge the gap between the physical systems being designed and the digital control systems that would run them.

280|

Fermilab

281|

The opportunity that would shape Bob's future came unexpectedly. A professor Bob worked for mentioned that his work at Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory in Chicago was looking for student engineers to help develop his experiments. The pay was good—and the experience would be unlike anything available on campus. Bob applied without expecting much. He was an undergraduate, after all, competing against graduate students for a position at one of the premier physics research facilities in the world. But his practical experience counted for something. The interviewers were less interested in his grades than in his ability to produce results, to understand systems from the component level up. He got the job.

282|

The summer after his junior year, Bob moved to a small apartment in Batavia, Illinois, and reported to work at a facility that looked like something from science fiction. The main accelerator ring was four miles in circumference, buried underground, a tunnel of superconducting magnets and particle detectors that probed the fundamental structure of matter.

283|

His job was more prosaic but no less important. The systems he developed, built from discrete transistors and early integrated circuits and 40 tons of iron plate, measured the energy of subatomic particles that existed for an unimaginably short time. Bob spent his days tracing signals through schematics, replacing components, redesigning subsystems. He worked alongside physicists and graduate students who were trying to understand the universe and who respected Bob for his practical ability to make things that worked.

284|

The experience was transformative in ways that classroom education couldn't be. At Fermilab, the stakes were real. When a control system failed, the accelerator shut down, and every hour of downtime cost thousands of dollars in lost research time. Bob learned to work under pressure, to diagnose problems quickly, to implement fixes that would hold. He learned to communicate with scientists who spoke a different language, to translate between the abstract goals of physics and the concrete constraints of engineering. He also learned that he was good at this—really good. The physicists sought his opinion on design decisions. The physicists requested him specifically when their equipment malfunctioned. He was, still an undergraduate, and he was contributing meaningfully to one of the most advanced scientific facilities in the world.

285|

The summer ended too quickly. Bob returned to Michigan State for his senior year with new confidence, new skills, and new clarity about what he wanted to do. He didn't want to be a physicist—he respected the science, but his talents lay in building the tools that made science possible. He wanted to design systems, create infrastructure, solve the practical problems that enabled others to push the boundaries of knowledge. More immediately, he wanted to return to Fermilab. The experience had been too valuable to be a one-time thing. He talked to his supervisors about returning after graduation, about making the temporary summer position into the beginning of a career. They were encouraging. The lab was growing, the systems were becoming more complex, and they needed people who combined theoretical knowledge with practical skills.

286|

The Departure

287|

The decision to leave Michigan after graduation carried emotional weight that Bob hadn't expected. He had spent his life in one town, in the orbit of his family, within reach of the garage and the kitchen and the familiar rhythms of home. Moving meant distance—not just physical, but the beginning of a separation that would only widen as he built his own life.

288|

His father was proud but quiet about the Fermilab opportunity. He had always imagined his son becoming an engineer, but the reality of it—Bob leaving, building a career in a world his father couldn't fully comprehend—brought a melancholy that he didn't know how to express. The garage had been their shared language, but Bob was learning new languages now, entering realms where his father's ability couldn't follow.

289|

His mother was more direct about her feelings. She cried when they said goodbye, then wiped her eyes.

290|

The Road Ahead

291|

Bob arrived at Fermilab in June, a newly minted graduate with a bachelor's degree in electrical engineering and two summer's worth of experience that had already proven he could do the work. The lab had grown in the year since he'd been there—new buildings, new equipment, new staff drawn from universities around the world. The main accelerator was running at higher energies, probing deeper into the structure of matter, generating data that would reshape physics. And Bob was part of it. Not in the spotlight—he would never be the physicist making discoveries or writing papers that changed how humanity understood the universe. But in the essential background. It was enough.

292|

Chapter 6: Life as an Engineer

304|

The first week was humbling. Bob made mistake after mistake, each one a small embarrassment that added up to a profound lesson in humility. Bob asked for "chips" and received what he would have called "fries." He asked for "pants" and nearly caused a shop assistant to blush. He tried to compliment a coworker's outfit and received a look of confusion—the words meant something different here. There were moments of genuine loneliness. Bob would sit in his Victorian hotel room, surrounded by travelers from a dozen different countries, and wonder what the hell he was doing there.

305|

But here's the thing about London: it grows on you. The more time I spent there, the more I understood its rhythms, its quirks, its secret beauty. Bob learned to love the pubs with their dark wood and warm beer—warm, yes, but somehow comforting in a way he never expected. He learned to navigate the Underground like a native, memorizing which lines connected where, understanding the peculiar etiquette of standing on the right and walking on the left.

306|

Bob made friends. Actual friends, among his coworker counterparts. They showed Bob the London they knew: the tucked-away cafes where the coffee was better than anything he'd had in America, the street markets where you could find anything if you looked hard enough, the parks where Londoners escaped the chaos of the city to read, relax, and pretend they weren't in one of the busiest places on Earth. Bob returned back to London many times since then. Each visit, he discovers something new. The city is like that—it keeps secrets, reveals them slowly, rewards patience.

307|

And that's a lesson Bob carried with him ever since. In business, in relationships, in everything—being a stranger in a strange land is the best education you can get. It teaches you humility. It teaches you patience. It teaches you that your way isn't the only way, and often isn't even the best way. As a result of London Bob became more curious about other cultures. More willing to ask questions instead of making assumptions. More comfortable being the outsider, knowing that discomfort was the price of growth.

308|

Nancy

309|

Bob met Nancy in a grocery store when he was visiting his company's HQ in Michigan. She was standing near the eggs when he arrived, he asked her if she was surprised by the high prices, as it was then—this was a time of high inflation and the price of eggs was up almost 100%. Bob and Nancy talked for a few minutes and then went their separate ways to check out and go home. By luck a few days later Bob was swimming in the apartment complex pool in the apartment office building and Nancy came by to pay her monthly rent. Bob recognized her and asked her on a date and that is how they met.

310|

Bob remembered his mother's advice, offered during a phone call when he had complained about feeling out of place: "You don't have to be the smartest person in the room, Bobby. You must be the most real. People remember that."

311|

She laughed again, and Bob felt something shift inside him, a recognition that this conversation was different from the dozens of polite exchanges he had endured at similar events. Nancy listened when he spoke—not waiting for her turn to talk, but actually hearing what he said, asking questions that showed she was following his thinking, engaging with his ideas rather than just his presence. They talked until the date ended.

312|

Courtship

313|

Their first date was awkward in the way of all first dates, two people feeling each other out, trying to present our best selves while concealing our uncertainties. Bob took her to a diner, a small place with good pie and bad coffee, where they talked until the waitress started giving them pointed looks. He learned that Nancy worked at a bank in the trust department. They discovered shared values—belief in the importance of work, respect for competence. They discovered complementary differences—her ease with people and words, his comfort with systems and machines.

314|

The second date was easier. The third was comfortable. By the fourth, they were finishing each other's sentences, laughing at jokes no one else would understand, that particular intimacy that emerges when two people recognize in each other something they didn't know they were seeking. Bob told her about his family—the father who didn't always know how to be soft, the mother who had taught him to see past the yelling. Nancy told him about her failed engagement, the man who had wanted her to be someone she wasn't, who had seen her literary ambitions as frivolous rather than essential.

315|

Building a Life

316|

Humility

317|

Not every lesson in adulthood arrived through achievement. One came wrapped in birthday paper. Bob had asked for a cordless drill to help with a boat-restoration project and opened the gift expecting exactly that. Instead he found a corded drill and, to his lasting embarrassment, let disappointment show plainly on his face. After the party his parents explained what he had not known: his father had lost his job, money was tight, and the drill on the table had been what they could afford.

318|

Bob felt ashamed at once. The point of the gift had never been the battery or the cord. It had been the effort, the intention, the love inside the limitation. He remembered that moment for the rest of his life and used it as a private check against entitlement. Accept gifts with grace. Be grateful for the thought before you judge the object. It was a small correction in the scale of a lifetime, but a permanent one.

319|

The Homebuilt Computer

320|

In 1979 Bob finally did something he had been moving toward since the IBM 1620 days: he built his own personal computer from a Heathkit design. By modern standards it was primitive—text only, floppy-disk storage, a keyboard, a display, and a dot-matrix printer. But that was beside the point. What mattered was ownership, intimacy, and the ability to know a machine not as a sealed appliance but as a thing assembled, understood, and improved by your own hands.

321|

To Bob it felt less like buying technology than joining it. He experimented for hours, learning what these new personal systems could and could not do, and quietly preparing himself for a future in which computing would move from specialist infrastructure into the center of ordinary business life. Long before the world called itself digital, Bob could already see where the current was flowing.

322|

They were married in the spring, a small ceremony in Michigan with Nancy's family and Bob's parents making awkward small talk across the cultural divide that separated their worlds. Bob's father, looking uncomfortable but proud. His mother cried, as mothers do.

323|

They bought a small house in Michigan with Bob commuting to Florida. It was the first time either of them had lived with another adult in a romantic partnership, and the learning curve was steep. Bob had to adjust to sharing space, to considering another person's preferences, to the give-and-take of domestic life. Nancy had to adjust to his long hours, his tendency to become absorbed in technical problems, his occasional withdrawal when work was frustrating. They fought, as all couples do. About small things—whose turn it was to do dishes, whether to spend money on new furniture or save for the future. About larger things—whether Bob was working too much, whether Nancy was too quick to accommodate his schedule at the expense of her own needs.

Chapter 9: The Y2K Challenge

The Night We Saved the World (Or At Least Our Little Corner of It)

504|

December 31, 1999. The entire world held its breath, waiting to see if computers would destroy civilization as we knew it.

505|

The Y2K bug—that harmless-sounding problem where computers might think the year 2000 was actually 1900—had become the center of everyone's attention. Newspapers ran scared stories about planes falling from the sky and power grids failing. People stockpiled supplies like apocalypse was coming. Some folks even built bomb shelters, convinced that the digital doomsday was finally at hand. And Bob? He was in his element—technology.

506|

As the CTO of a growing tech company, Bob was responsible for making sure the business systems would survive the night. For months, Bob's team had been testing, patching, updating—doing everything we could to ensure the software wouldn't crash when the clock struck midnight. Bob spent countless nights in the server room with his team, chasing down legacy code written by programmers long gone, trying to understand the logic (or illogic) of systems built decades ago.

507|

Bob remembers gathering his team in the server room on New Year's Eve. The mood was tense but focused. They had done everything they could. Now they just had to wait. The server room was cold—that particular air-conditioned chill that computers love but humans tolerate. Banks of monitors flickered with green text, showing system status after system status. The hum of cooling fans was the only sound besides our breathing.

508|

The hours crawled by. At 11:30 PM, they started their final checks. All systems: green. At 11:55, they gathered around a single monitor displaying the clock.

509|

Five... four... three... two... one...

510|

The year changed to 2000. And nothing happened.

511|

The systems kept running. The world kept spinning. The great Y2K apocalypse had fizzled into a damp whimper.

512|

What Y2K Taught Bob

513|

In the aftermath, there were lots of jokes about the whole thing being overblown. The media had scared everyone for nothing. All that preparation, all that worry, and it turned out to be a whole lot of nothing. And maybe it was. Maybe all that preparation was unnecessary. Maybe the boogeyman wasn't real.

514|

But here's what Bob learned: it's better to be prepared and not need it than to need it and not be prepared. That lesson has stayed with him throughout his career. Bob has seen companies cut corners on testing, skip the boring but necessary maintenance, assume everything will be fine because it's always been fine. And Bob watched them crash and burn in spectacular ways that could have been prevented with a little foresight.

515|

The Y2K bug was a collective victory for the tech industry. They came together, worked hard, and solved a problem before it became a crisis. It wasn't glamorous work—there were no press conferences, no victory parades, just a bunch of tired engineers drinking bad coffee and staring at screens. But it mattered. It mattered a lot.

516|

More importantly, Bob learned that fear is not a good reason to do nothing. The world was terrified of Y2K, but we didn't let that fear paralyze us. We acted, we prepared, and we succeeded. Fear is just an emotion. What you do with it—that's what counts.
